title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 8: The Inspiration of the Judiciary
primary_topics: Chapter 8 of 'A Centenary of Justice' -- an 'Inspirational Message' CJP delivered on January 27, 2001 at the Waterfront Hotel in Cebu City during Region 7's 'Culmination Night,' offered as a sustained character portrait of CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr. as the model the judiciary should emulate

A definition of inspiration (Webster's 'act or power of moving the intellect or emotion') and the thesis that 'true leadership is sourced from example and inspiration, not from force and domination' -- leadership-by-example
Davide profiled in four virtues: (1) integrity and moral courage, (2) simple, frugal and transparent living, (3) dedication to duty, and (4) deep faith in Jesus Christ

Davide's Bible-cutting practice and two providential readings -- 2 Maccabees 10 ('Purification of the Temple') on his Nov 30, 1998 appointment, inspiring his mission to cleanse the judiciary, and Isaiah 62 ('Restoration of Zion') on Jan 20, 2001, the day he decided to swear in President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo at the EDSA Shrine
sub_topics: The occasion: Region VII 'blazes the trail' as the first region to celebrate, fittingly so since CJ Davide hails from the area; CJP thanks Judges Galicano C. Arriesgado, Isaias Dicdican and Pampio Abarintos for the invitation

Defining inspiration: distinguishing the Christian sense (divine influence enabling the gospel writers) from Webster's secondary sense, 'an act or power of moving the intellect or emotion'; quoting Longfellow -- 'Lives of great men all remind us we can make our life sublime'

The leadership thesis: 'true leadership is sourced from example and inspiration, not from force and domination'; to be inspired is to be led by the example of an admired model -- in the judiciary, CJ Davide

Virtue 1 -- integrity and moral courage: in ten years as a jurist (and before as legislator, constitution-maker and elections chairman) no taint of corruption; 'no business cronies, no favored friends, no officious relatives'; 'what political will is to a sovereign head, moral courage is to a magistrate' -- a judge who knows all the law but lacks moral courage 'is really nothing'

Virtue 2 -- simple, frugal, transparent living: Davide 'does not drink, does not smoke, does not gamble,' wakes about 3:30 a.m. to pray, brisk-walks, and is humble and soft-spoken yet self-actualized -- 'I have yet to hear him raise his voice'

Virtue 3 -- dedication to duty: reports to office at 5:30 a.m., an 'elephantine memory' and 'gluttonous appetite' for judicial work; writes exhaustively, 'dissecting issues with a surgeon's scalpel,' avoiding 'obiters, flamboyance and braggadocio'; simultaneously ran his CJ work and presided over the Impeachment Court
Virtue 4 -- spirituality and faith: Davide's practice of cutting the Bible at random each morning for the day's instruction, believing himself 'simply the Lord's servant'

The Nov 30, 1998 appointment: the Bible opened to 2 Maccabees 10, 'Purification of the Temple and the City,' which he took as God's call to 'purify and cleanse the judiciary of the misfit, the corrupt and the unqualified' and to 'welcome and reward the competent and the ethical'

January 20, 2001: the Bible opened to Isaiah 62, 'Restoration of Zion'; reflecting on the ongoing EDSA II, Davide resolved to induct Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo as the 14th President at the EDSA Shrine -- 'the culmination of the EDSA II People Power Revolt'

The exhortation and acclaim: CJP urges the judiciary to follow Davide's example; the 'normally critical' Philippine Daily Inquirer had named Davide 'Filipino of the Year' and polls rated him the most admired citizen -- a model 'not only for the here and now, but also for the hereafter and forever'

stances.claim: True leadership is 'sourced from example and inspiration, not from force and domination'; people accomplish heroic deeds because they are moved by the words and lives of others, so the judiciary's reform depends less on command than on an admired model -- embodied in CJ Davide.
stances.rhetorical_move: leadership-by-example thesis (the organizing premise of CJP's whole Davide corpus), grounded in Longfellow and in a definition of 'inspiration' as the power to move intellect and emotion
stances.confidence: asserted as the governing claim of the address

stances.claim: Moral courage is the indispensable judicial virtue: 'what political will is to a sovereign head, moral courage is to a magistrate.' A judge may have memorized the Constitution, the codes, the UN Charter and the UDHR, but without the willingness 'to battle the establishment' and 'stand for his conviction against all odds,' even against all his colleagues, 'he is really nothing.' And moral courage is born of integrity -- only the pure of heart 'with no skeletons to hide' can possess it.
stances.rhetorical_move: moral-courage-over-erudition: subordinating doctrinal mastery to character, with integrity framed as the precondition of courage
stances.confidence: asserted as a definition of judicial greatness, exemplified by Davide

notable_anecdotes: The Bible-cutting practice: Davide wakes about 3:30 a.m., prays, then 'cuts the Bible and reads at random the page that opens,' believing himself 'simply the Lord's servant who gets his day-to-day instruction from God's book.'

2 Maccabees on appointment day: on November 30, 1998 the random page was 2 Maccabees 10, titled 'Purification of the Temple and the City' -- which Davide took as his mandate to cleanse the judiciary of 'the misfit, the corrupt and the unqualified' and reward 'the competent and the ethical.'

Isaiah on EDSA II day: on January 20, 2001 the page opened to Isaiah 62, 'Restoration of Zion'; reflecting on the ongoing EDSA People Power, Davide resolved that very day to swear in Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo as the 14th President at the EDSA Shrine.

The frugal, even-tempered Chief: Davide 'does not drink, does not smoke, does not gamble,' has 'no business cronies, no favored friends, no officious relatives,' and in more than five years together CJP had 'yet to hear him raise his voice'; he reports to office at 5:30 a.m. and writes 'dissecting issues with a surgeon's scalpel.'

Dual duty during the impeachment: people marveled that Davide could do his Chief Justice work in the mornings and preside over the Impeachment Court in the afternoons and evenings, both 'in a brilliant and faultless manner.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces the 'Inspirational Message' CJP delivered on January 27, 2001 at the Waterfront Hotel in Cebu City during Region VII's 'Culmination Night' -- fittingly the first region to celebrate, since CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr. hails from there. Defining inspiration (after Webster) as 'an act or power of moving the intellect or emotion' and quoting Longfellow that 'lives of great men all remind us we can make our life sublime,' CJP argues that 'true leadership is sourced from example and inspiration, not from force and domination,' and offers Davide as the judiciary's model in four virtues. First, integrity and moral courage: in a decade as jurist (and earlier as legislator, constitution-maker and elections chairman) no corruption ever touched him -- 'no business cronies, no favored friends, no officious relatives' -- and 'what political will is to a sovereign head, moral courage is to a magistrate,' so that a judge who has memorized the Constitution and the UDHR but lacks the courage to stand against the establishment 'is really nothing.' Second, simple, frugal, transparent living: Davide 'does not drink, does not smoke, does not gamble,' wakes near 3:30 a.m. to pray, and is soft-spoken yet self-actualized. Third, dedication: he reports at 5:30 a.m., writes exhaustively 'dissecting issues with a surgeon's scalpel,' and ran his CJ duties while brilliantly presiding over the Impeachment Court. Fourth, faith: his practice of cutting the Bible each morning for the day's instruction yielded two providential readings -- 2 Maccabees 10 ('Purification of the Temple') on his November 30, 1998 appointment, inspiring his mission to cleanse the judiciary and reward the competent and ethical, and Isaiah 62 ('Restoration of Zion') on January 20, 2001, the day he resolved to swear in Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo as the 14th President at the EDSA Shrine. CJP closes by urging the judiciary to follow this example -- a Chief whom the 'normally critical' Philippine Daily Inquirer had named 'Filipino of the Year' and polls rated the most admired citizen -- 'not only for the here and now, but also for the hereafter and forever.'
